question: What is the difference between struct and class in Swift?
answer:
A struct is a value type and a class is a reference type; almost every other difference follows from that one.

• struct — copied on assignment and on every function call. No inheritance. Free memberwise initializer. Methods that change stored properties must be marked `mutating`. Small ones live on the stack or inline in their container.
• class — shared by reference and counted by ARC. Supports inheritance, `deinit`, and identity comparison with `===`. Always heap-allocated.

Use struct by default. Reach for class only when you need something a value cannot provide: identity that many owners must share, inheritance, `deinit` for cleanup, or `AnyObject` conformance for Objective-C interop and `weak` references.

Concurrency has sharpened the rule. A struct of Sendable properties is Sendable for free, while a class with `var` properties is not — sharing one across tasks is a compile error under the Swift 6 language mode unless you make it an actor, make it immutable, or take a lock and claim `@unchecked Sendable`.

question: What are protocols in Swift and how are they different from interfaces?
answer:
A protocol declares a contract — methods, properties, associated types, initializers — that conforming types must implement.

Differences vs Java/C# interfaces:
• Both classes AND value types (struct, enum) can conform.
• Protocols can have associated types — generic-like type parameters (`associatedtype Item`).
• Protocol extensions can provide default implementations and add methods to all conformers without modifying their source.
• Existentials (`any Protocol`) are runtime-erased boxes; opaque types (`some Protocol`) are compile-time concrete.

Protocol-oriented programming (POP) is Swift's idiomatic answer to inheritance.

question: Explain enums with associated values and raw values in Swift.
answer:
A Swift enum is a full type that can carry data, which is why it models a closed set of alternatives far better than a set of integer constants.

• Raw values — every case maps to the same underlying primitive (Int, String, Character). The compiler synthesises `RawRepresentable`, giving you `HTTPStatus(rawValue: 404)` and `.ok.rawValue`. Note the initializer is failable, because an unknown raw value has no case.
• Associated values — each case carries its own typed payload, and different cases can carry different payloads. That is what makes an enum an algebraic data type, and it is the right shape for screen state, parser tokens, and anything with a "loading / loaded / failed" life.

A case can have raw values or associated values, never both.

Enums are value types and can carry methods, computed properties, static members and protocol conformances just like a struct. Pair them with `switch`, which the compiler checks for exhaustiveness — add a case and every switch that forgot it fails to compile, which is the whole point.

`indirect` allows recursive cases (a tree, a linked list) by boxing the payload behind a pointer.

question: What are extensions in Swift and what can/can't they do?
answer:
Extensions add functionality to an existing type — your own types, standard library types, even types imported from a framework — without subclassing and without touching the original source.

Can add:
• Computed properties (instance and static)
• Methods (instance, static, and `mutating`)
• Initializers (convenience initializers for classes)
• Subscripts
• Protocol conformance, including conditional conformance
• Nested types

Cannot add:
• Stored properties — there is no room for them in the original type's memory layout
• Overrides of existing methods — an extension adds, it never replaces
• A designated initializer on a class you do not own

One Swift 6 wrinkle: conforming an imported type to an imported protocol (`extension URL: Identifiable`) is a retroactive conformance, and the compiler now warns about it, because the owning module could add the same conformance later and the two would collide. Spell it `extension URL: @retroactive Identifiable` to acknowledge the risk, or wrap the type instead.

Idiomatic uses: split a large type into feature-sized chunks, conform a type you do not own to a protocol you do own, add helpers to Array and String, and keep protocol default implementations out of the protocol declaration.

question: What is protocol-oriented programming and how is it different from class inheritance?
answer:
Protocol-oriented programming (POP) — a Swift idiom championed at WWDC 2015 — composes behavior via small protocols and default implementations rather than deep class hierarchies.

Why POP over class inheritance:
• Works with structs and enums, not just classes
• Multiple conformance — a type can adopt many protocols, sidestepping single-inheritance
• Composition over inheritance — features added in tiny chunks (Equatable, Hashable, Identifiable) and mixed at will
• Better testability — protocols become natural mock boundaries
• No fragile-base-class problem

When to keep inheritance: deep frameworks (UIView/NSObject), Cocoa/UIKit interop, override-based template methods.

question: Explain access control levels in Swift.
answer:
Swift has six access levels, and a member is always capped by the visibility of the type that contains it.

From most to least visible:
• open — visible everywhere AND subclassable/overridable from another module. Classes and their members only.
• public — visible from any module, but subclassing and overriding are limited to the defining module.
• package — visible from any target in the same Swift package. Fills the gap between `internal` and `public` for multi-module packages.
• internal (the default) — visible inside the current module only.
• fileprivate — visible inside the same source file.
• private — visible inside the enclosing declaration and its extensions in the same file.

The containment rule catches people out: a `public` method on an `internal` type is effectively internal, and a `public` function cannot expose an `internal` type in its signature. Initializers default to `internal`, which is why a `public struct` from a package is not constructible from outside until you write `public init`.

Start closed and widen deliberately. `private` by default keeps the invariants of a type inside the type, and a small `public` surface is the only thing that makes a module's API reviewable.

question: What are property observers and lazy properties?
answer:
Swift lets a stored property carry behaviour in two ways: observers that fire around a change, and `lazy`, which defers the initializer until the first read.

• willSet / didSet — run just before and just after the value changes. `willSet` sees `newValue`, `didSet` sees `oldValue`. They only apply to stored properties, and they do NOT fire when you assign from inside the type's own initializer.
• lazy — the initializer runs on first access, not at init time. It must be a `var` (the storage is written on first read), it can refer to `self`, and it is not thread-safe: two concurrent first-reads can run the initializer twice.
• Computed property — no storage at all; the getter runs on every access and an optional setter runs on every assignment.

Pick by intent: observers for side effects on change (invalidate a layout, fire analytics), `lazy` for an expensive default you may never need, computed for a value that is always derivable from other state.

Two traps worth remembering. Observers fire on every assignment, even when the new value equals the old one, so guard with `oldValue` when the work is expensive. And a `lazy` property is a mutation, so reading one on a `let` struct instance will not compile.
